solutions.latex:
As $y=2x+1$ is a tangent at $x=-1$, then $f'(-1)=2$

$$\begin{aligned}(-1)^2+k\times(-1)&=2\\1-k&=2\\k&=-1\end{aligned}$$

$$\int f'(x)\,dx=f(x),\qquad f(x)=\dfrac{x^3}{3}-\dfrac{x^2}{2}+C$$

Point needed: $x=-1,\ y=2(-1)+1=-1$

$\therefore f(-1)=-1$

$$\begin{aligned}f(-1)=-1&=\dfrac{(-1)^3}{3}-\dfrac{(-1)^2}{2}+C\\-1&=-\dfrac{1}{3}-\dfrac{1}{2}+C\\C&=-\dfrac{1}{6}\end{aligned}$$

$$f(x)=\dfrac{x^3}{3}-\dfrac{x^2}{2}-\dfrac{1}{6}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 3: marks circled in the scan at $k=-1$, at $f(x)=\frac{x^3}{3}-\frac{x^2}{2}+C$, at $f(-1)=-1$ and at $C=-\frac{1}{6}$ (four marks circled for three, with an 'OR' drawn beside them)

solutions.question: 12(d)
solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=3x^2-2x-1\\&=(3x+1)(x-1)\end{aligned}$$

Stationary points when $f'(x)=0$

$$0=(3x+1)(x-1)$$

$x=-\dfrac{1}{3}$ or $x=1$

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x&-1&-\frac{1}{3}&0&1&2\\\hline f'(x)&4&0&-1&0&7\\\hline\end{array}$$

Shape of the gradient: $/\ \ \overline{\phantom{xx}}\ \ \backslash\ \ \underline{\phantom{xx}}\ \ /$, so a maximum at $x=-\dfrac{1}{3}$ and a minimum at $x=1$.

$f\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)=\dfrac{5}{27}$, so $\left(-\dfrac{1}{3},\dfrac{5}{27}\right)$ is a maximum turning point.

$f(1)=-1$, so $(1,-1)$ is a minimum turning point.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 3: 1 for $f'(x)=3x^2-2x-1$; 1 for the nature test (table of $f'(x)$, or $f''(x)$); 1 for the coordinates and nature of both points

solutions.question: 14(e)
solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}49&=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta\\98&=r^2\theta\\\theta&=\dfrac{98}{r^2}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}P&=2r+r\theta\\&=2r+r\times\dfrac{98}{r^2}\\P&=2r+98r^{-1}\\\dfrac{dP}{dr}&=2-1\times 98\times r^{-2}\\&=2-\dfrac{98}{r^2}\end{aligned}$$

Turning point when $\dfrac{dP}{dr}=0$

$$\begin{aligned}0&=2-\dfrac{98}{r^2}\\0&=2r^2-98\\r^2&=49\\r&=\pm 7\end{aligned}$$

$r=7$ as $r>0$

$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2P}{dr^2}&=-2\times -1\times 98\times r^{-3}\\&=196r^{-3}\end{aligned}$$

When $r=7$, $\dfrac{d^2P}{dr^2}=0.57\ldots>0$

$\therefore r=7$ is when $P$ is a minimum.

Arc length $=7\times\dfrac{98}{7^2}=14=2\times 7$

$\therefore$ diameter $=$ arc length, for minimum perimeter.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 4: 1 for $\theta=\frac{98}{r^2}$; 1 for $P=2r+98r^{-1}$; 1 for $r=7$ (as $r>0$) from $\frac{dP}{dr}=0$; 1 for arc length $=14=2\times 7$

To get from $f(x)\to g(x)$:

\begin{itemize}
\item H.D. $\dfrac{1}{4}$
\item H.T. left $1$
\item V.D. $-2$
\item V.T. up $1$
\end{itemize}

Reverse for $(4,21)$:

\begin{itemize}
\item Down $1$: $(4,20)$
\item V.D. $-\dfrac{1}{2}$: $(4,-10)$
\item Right $1$: $(5,-10)$
\item H.D. $4$: $(20,-10)$
\end{itemize}

Alternative:

$$\begin{aligned}g(4)=21&=-2\times f(4\times 4+4)+1\\21&=-2f(20)+1\\20&=-2f(20)\\-10&=f(20)\end{aligned}$$

$(20,-10)$

$y=1$ and $y=-x^2+1$ are both continuous and differentiable for all real $x$.

$x=0,\ f(0)=1$ and $-x^2+1=-0^2+1=1$

$\therefore$ continuous

$x=0$: $f'(0)=0$

$$\begin{aligned}y&=-x^2+1\\y'&=-2x\end{aligned}$$

$x=0:\ y'=0=f'(x)$

$\therefore$ differentiable.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 2: 1 for showing continuity at $x=0$ (both pieces give 1); 1 for showing differentiability (both gradients are 0)
